lead: A screen that shows a list never copies its data into the view. The view asks a data source how many rows exist, and asks again for each row just before that row appears. Controls run the other way: a switch, slider or text field fires an event and your code reacts to it. This asking and reacting pair is how nearly every iOS screen works — a fare list, a route picker, a profile photo, a share menu. This chapter builds that loop with UITableView, UIPickerView, UIImageView, UIMenu and control events.
prereq: You need: functions and closures from 6.2, and outlets and actions from 6.5.

sections.h3: A table view asks for rows on demand

blocks.text: UITableView shows a scrolling list and stores no data of its own. It holds two connections to your view controller: dataSource and delegate. Both are protocols, meaning a list of methods a class promises to implement. The data source answers "how many rows" and "what goes in this row". The delegate answers "the user did something".

Two data source methods are required. tableView(_:numberOfRowsInSection:) returns an Int, the row count for the section number passed in. tableView(_:cellForRowAt:) returns one configured UITableViewCell. IndexPath carries two Int fields, section and row, both counting from 0. Row 1 is the second row, not the first.

items: The table view calls numberOfRowsInSection once per section to learn the counts.
It calls cellForRowAt only for rows near the visible area, not for all rows.
Inside that method, call dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:) to take a recycled cell from the reuse pool.
Fill the cell's labels from the model array, using indexPath.row as the index.
Return the cell; the table places it on screen.
When the array changes, call tableView.reloadData() so the table asks again.

blocks.text: Reuse is why the identifier matters. A cell scrolled off the bottom returns to the pool, and a cell scrolled into view is pulled out of it. The identifier string in code must equal the prototype cell's Identifier in the storyboard. If they differ, the app stops with the message "unable to dequeue a cell with identifier".

didSelectRowAt fires on a tap. Read indexPath.row, look up the model, and pass that one value onward. For a custom layout, subclass UITableViewCell, connect its label outlets, and cast the dequeued cell: let cell = tableView.dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier: "FareCell", for: indexPath) as! FareCell.

UIPickerView is a spinning wheel. It has components (columns) numbered from 0, and each component has rows. The data source returns numberOfComponents and pickerView(_:numberOfRowsInComponent:). The delegate returns pickerView(_:titleForRow:forComponent:) and receives didSelectRow. That is the same ask-don't-push pattern as the table.

UIImage is the in-memory bitmap; UIImageView draws it. Put image files in the asset catalogue (Assets.xcassets) so Xcode supplies the right scale. Load with UIImage(named: "chennai"), with no file extension. contentMode decides how the image fits its frame: .scaleAspectFit keeps the ratio and leaves empty space, .scaleAspectFill keeps the ratio and crops, .scaleToFill stretches and distorts.

UIMenu and UIAction build a pop-up menu without a storyboard. An action has a title, an optional image, and a handler closure (see 6.2). Group actions in a UIMenu, then attach it: button.menu = menu and button.showsMenuAsPrimaryAction = true, or barButtonItem.menu = menu. Some syllabi call this using menus with views.

Controls report change through events. In Interface Builder you drag from the control to your code and choose the event. In code you call addTarget(_:action:for:). The handler usually takes the sender, for example @IBAction func fareChanged(_ sender: UISlider) { label.text = String(sender.value) }.

items: UISwitch fires .valueChanged; read its isOn Bool.
UISlider fires .valueChanged; read value as a Float, bounded by minimumValue and maximumValue.
UISegmentedControl fires .valueChanged; read selectedSegmentIndex, an Int counting from 0.
UITextField fires .editingChanged on every keystroke and .editingDidEnd when editing stops; read text, a String?.

blocks.text: Three supporting views appear on most screens. UIScrollView scrolls content larger than the screen. UIStackView arranges children in a row or a column and is the usual way to build a form (see 6.7). UIActivityIndicatorView is a spinner: call startAnimating() before slow work and stopAnimating() after. For a message, build a UIAlertController, add a UIAlertAction, then present(_:animated:completion:).

The rule holds everywhere: the view asks the model for data at the moment it needs it. Data never pushes itself into a view. You change the array, then call reloadData() or set the label, and the view redraws.

spec.aria: Three trips worked out to 92, 158 and 65 in an array with indices 0 to 2; a table view with three rows, the middle one highlighted showing 158; a box shows the tap passing 158 onward.

examples.question: A cab app charges a base fare of ₹20 plus distance × rate per km. The city rate is ₹9.0 per km; the outstation rate is ₹11.5 per km. Three trips are booked in a one-section table: 8 km city, 12 km outstation, 5 km city. (i) Compute each fare. (ii) What does numberOfRowsInSection return? (iii) What does the cell at indexPath.row = 1 display? (iv) The user taps that row — what value must the next screen receive?
steps: The model array is [92, 158, 65]. It has 3 elements, and the table has one section, so numberOfRowsInSection returns 3.
The table calls cellForRowAt for indexPath.row = 1. The index picks the second element, so the cell shows ₹158.
didSelectRowAt records indexPath.section = 0 and indexPath.row = 1, reads fares[1] = 158, and passes 158 to the next screen, not the whole array.
examples.answer: The fares are ₹92, ₹158 and ₹65; the table has 3 rows; row 1 shows ₹158; the tap passes the single value 158 onward.
examples.check:
base = 20.0
trips = [(8, 9.0), (12, 11.5), (5, 9.0)]
fares = [base + km * rate for km, rate in trips]
for f in fares:
    print(int(f))
print(len(fares))
print(int(fares[1]))

examples.question: Second short check: a slider has minimumValue 0 and maximumValue 100 and sits at 37.5. The handler is label.text = String(sender.value). What does the label show, and how do you print it to one decimal place?
steps: String(37.5) gives the shortest exact description, so the label shows 37.5.
For a fixed decimal count, build a formatter or use String(format: "%.1f", sender.value), which also gives 37.5.
Setting .valueChanged as the event means the label updates on every drag, not only on release.
Store minimumValue = 0 and maximumValue = 100 on the slider so the Float stays in range.
examples.answer: The label shows 37.5 in both cases, but String(format: "%.1f", ...) guarantees exactly one decimal place.

traps: Using indexPath.section where indexPath.row belongs. With one section the code still works, so the bug appears only when a second section is added.
The reuse identifier in code not matching the prototype cell in the storyboard. The app stops with "unable to dequeue a cell with identifier".
Re-sorting or filtering the model array inside cellForRowAt, so row numbers no longer match the data. Sort once, outside the method.
Returning a recycled cell without resetting every label, so an old row's text flashes in a new row. Always overwrite all labels.

A storyboard action or outlet still connected to a method or property you renamed or deleted. The app crashes on unrecognized selector when the control fires. Delete the old connection and reconnect it.

quiz.q: Name the two required methods of UITableViewDataSource.
Why does a table view call cellForRowAt only for rows near the visible area?
quiz.a: A list can hold thousands of rows while the screen shows ten. Building only visible cells saves memory and time; offscreen cells wait in the reuse pool and are handed back through dequeueReusableCell.

quiz.q: An array of 4 names fills a two-section table, two rows per section. What does numberOfRowsInSection return for section 1, and which array element does indexPath (section 1, row 0) show?
quiz.a: It returns 2. Section 1, row 0 is the first row of the second group, so it shows names[2] if you index as section * 2 + row. Working it out: 1 × 2 + 0 = 2.

quiz.q: A student sorts the fares array in place after the table loads but never calls reloadData(). Explain what the screen shows and what a tap now passes onward.
quiz.a: The table keeps the cells it already drew, so the old order stays on screen. A tap reads indexPath.row for the row the user sees, then looks up the re-sorted array at that same index, so it opens a different trip than the row on screen. If rows were also deleted without reloadData(), the index can run past the end and crash.

quiz.q: Which contentMode keeps an image's aspect ratio and leaves empty space around it?
quiz.a: .scaleAspectFit. .scaleAspectFill also keeps the ratio but crops, and .scaleToFill stretches.

.valueChanged belongs to controls such as sliders, switches and segmented controls and fires when their value changes. .editingChanged fires on a text field on every keystroke while the user is typing.

quiz.q: A bar button item already has a UIMenu assigned, yet nothing appears when it is tapped. Give two likely causes.
quiz.a: The menu's UIAction list is empty, or its actions have nil titles and no handler, so the menu has nothing to show. Or the menu was assigned to a different bar button item than the one on screen. Separate note: showsMenuAsPrimaryAction matters only for a plain UIButton, which needs it set to true; a bar button item shows its menu on tap without it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern iOS code often replaces reloadData() with a diffable data source (UITableViewDiffableDataSource and NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot), which animates insertions and deletions and removes the index arithmetic that causes most row bugs. UICollectionView with compositional layout generalises the same data source idea to grids and complex screens. SwiftUI goes further: a List reads an array, and a @State property change redraws the body automatically. Menus also grew: deferred menus, submenus and context menus on long press. Search next for "UITableViewDiffableDataSource", "SwiftUI List" and "UIMenu deferred menu".
